docs.title: Friction log: Claude API (Messages API + tool use)
docs.text:
Notes from building Kairos; to be expanded.

Things that slowed me down while porting the Gemini calendar agent to Claude. SDK: anthropic 2.13.0 (Python). Model used for testing: set via CLAUDE_MODEL (Switch models). The code is claude_agent.py; the API comparison is in PORTING.md.

Format per entry: what I tried / what happened / what I expected / suggested fix.

docs.title: 1. Choosing between the Tool Runner and a manual loop
docs.text:
• Tried: Looked up the "tool use loop" for Python to mirror the Gemini flow.
  • Happened: The docs lead with the Tool Runner (client.beta.messages.tool_runner, @beta_tool) as the recommended path; the manual loop is presented as the fallback. The runner is a beta API, and it hides the request/response round-trip I wanted to show side by side with Gemini.
  • Expected: A short "which one should I use?" table up front: runner for most apps, manual loop when you need a custom confirmation step, want no beta dependency, or are teaching the loop.
  • Suggested fix: Add that decision table at the top of the tool-use page, and show that a human-approval step works in both (the runner's docs mention it in one line).

docs.title: 2. strict: true means the schema can't be shared verbatim
docs.text:
• Tried: Reusing the exact JSON Schema object from the Gemini tool, and turning on strict: true so Claude's arguments are guaranteed to validate.
  • Happened: Strict mode requires additionalProperties: false on the schema, so the shared schema needs a Claude-specific tweak ({**TOOL_PARAMETERS, "additionalProperties": False}).
  • Expected: Either the API to assume additionalProperties: false under strict mode, or a clear error message saying exactly what to add.
  • Suggested fix: Put the additionalProperties: false requirement in the first strict-mode example, not just the reference text.

docs.title: 3. The response isn't just [tool_use]: thinking blocks come first
docs.text:
• Tried: Pulling Claude's text with response.content[0].text, the way many quick examples do.
  • Happened: On current models thinking is on by default, so content can start with a thinking block (with empty text unless you opt into summaries). Indexing [0] gives the wrong block type.
  • Expected: Examples that never rely on block position.
  • Suggested fix: Have every quickstart filter by block.type == "text" / "tool_use", and note that the whole response.content (thinking included) must be sent back as the assistant turn.

docs.title: 4. tool_result content is the opposite of Gemini's rule
docs.text:
• Tried: Sending the event result dict back as the tool result, as the Gemini agent does.
  • Happened: Claude's tool_result.content takes a string or a list of content blocks, so the dict has to be json.dumps()-ed. Gemini's Interactions API is the reverse: it wants the raw dict, and a JSON string caused problems (see the Gemini log).
  • Expected: Not friction in Claude's API on its own, but a sharp edge when porting.
  • Suggested fix: A "coming from other providers" note on the tool-use page listing the result format difference.

docs.title: 5. No default model, so you need to know a current id
docs.text:
• Tried: Following the plan's rule of no hard-coded model (CLAUDE_MODEL from env).
  • Happened: Fine once set, but a newcomer has to find a current model id first, and ids from older tutorials may be retired.
  • Expected: An easy way to discover a valid id.
  • Suggested fix: Point newcomers at client.models.list() in the quickstart so they can print the available ids.

docs.title: Friction log: Claude API quickstart and Messages API guide (Python)
docs.text:
Notes from following Anthropic's documentation site while trying the Messages API, before building Kairos. Rewritten from my own notes; the examples are from the docs as they were on the date below.

Date: 2026-11-25 Goal: Make a first API call by following the docs, then try the examples in "Using the Messages API" (basic request, multi-turn, prefill, vision). Pages followed: - Claude docs home (starting point): https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/home - Get started: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/get-started - Using the Messages API: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages

Environment:

Component Version OS macOS 26.6.2 (Darwin 25.6.0), Apple silicon Python 3.9.6 (macOS system python3) → 3.12.13 (Homebrew), after the fix in issue 1 anthropic Python SDK 0.125.0 → 2.14.0, after the fix in issue 1 httpx2 not installed → 2.16.2 (installed with SDK 2.14.0) ant CLI 2.14.0 (Homebrew) Editor VS Code with Pylance Virtual environment Created with the command from Get started (python3 -m venv .venv)

Severity scale: High = copied code fails or I could not continue without outside help. Medium = it worked, but I was confused or unsure what was happening. Low = minor annoyance.

docs.title: Top 3 takeaways
docs.text:
1. Setup gives you an old SDK without warning. On the default macOS Python (3.9), pip install anthropic falls back to SDK 0.125.0, which then breaks the vision example's import httpx2.
  2. Examples steer you toward high cost and old models. Every example defaults to the most expensive model, with no cost guidance, and the prefill example runs on a deprecated one.
  3. Credential precedence and billing need plain language. When both ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ant auth login are set up, the docs don't say which credential is used or which organization is billed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: # Page Issue Severity 1 Get started pip install anthropic silently installs an old SDK on Python 3.9; no Python version requirement is given High 2 Using the Messages API Vision example's import httpx2 fails with the SDK that step 1 installs High 3 Get started Using both an API key and ant auth login gives a warning the page doesn't explain; unclear which account is billed Medium 4 Both Every example uses Claude Opus 5.5 with no cost guidance or pointer to cheaper models Medium 5 Using the Messages API Prefill example runs on a deprecated model; no runnable version for current models Medium 6 Using the Messages API Code snippets leave out import anthropic Low 7 Using the Messages API Python output looks different from the JSON shown on the page Low 8 Using the Messages API Vision example gives no way to see the image Claude is describing Low 9 Get started Sample output says "Renewable energy news 2025" Low

docs.title: 1. pip install anthropic silently installs an old SDK (High)
docs.text:
Page: Get started, Python tab, step "Create a project and install the SDK"

What I did: Ran the commands as written: 

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install anthropic

What happened: On macOS, python3 is 3.9.6. pip installed anthropic 0.125.0 without any warning. The latest release on PyPI is 2.14.0, which requires Python 3.10 or later, so pip quietly fell back to the last version that supports 3.9. I only found this out later, while debugging issue 2.

Expected: A stated Python version requirement, or a check before the install step.

How I fixed it: Rebuilt the virtual environment with Homebrew's Python 3.12 (python3.12 -m venv --clear .venv) and ran pip install anthropic again. That installed 2.14.0, and the docs' import httpx2 then worked unchanged.

Suggestion: Add a prerequisite such as "Python 3.10 or later. Check with python3 --version." Include a macOS note, because the system Python is 3.9. Consider showing how to confirm the installed SDK version (pip show anthropic).

docs.title: 2. Vision example: import httpx2 cannot be resolved (High)
docs.text:
Page: Using the Messages API, Vision section, Python tab

What I did: Copied the Python vision example, which starts with: 

import base64
import httpx2

What happened: Pylance reported Import "httpx2" could not be resolved (reportMissingImports). The SDK that issue 1 installed (0.125.0) depends on httpx, not httpx2, so httpx2 isn't installed. Running the script would fail with ModuleNotFoundError. At first this looked like a typo in the docs, and I changed it to import httpx. That works only because of the old SDK.

Expected: Code from the docs works with the SDK that the docs' own install step gives me.

Suggestion: Say that httpx2 comes with newer versions of the anthropic SDK, and link to the Python version requirement. Alternatively, download the image with the standard library (urllib.request) so the example has no extra dependency.

docs.title: 3. API key and CLI login conflict; unclear which account is billed (Medium)
docs.text:
Page: Get started, "Choose how to authenticate"

What I did: At different times I set up both options on the page: I exported ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and also ran ant auth login.

What happened: I got this message:

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set and takes precedence over the SDK's profile / federation auto-discovery; unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to use the auto-discovered credential.

I didn't know what "profile / federation auto-discovery" meant, which credential my scripts were using, or which account was paying. ant auth status showed that the API key was active and the login profile was being ignored. The key and the login belonged to two different organizations. To confirm which one was billed, I had to call the API and read the anthropic-organization-id response header.

Expected: The page says "Follow the steps for one of the following options" but doesn't say what happens if both are set up.

Suggestion: Add a note to this step: "If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, it is used instead of your CLI login. Run ant auth status to see which credential is active. Usage is billed to the organization that owns the active credential." Reword the warning in plain language, or link from it to the Authentication page.

docs.title: 4. No cost guidance; every example uses the most expensive default (Medium)
docs.text:
Pages: Get started; Using the Messages API

What happened: Every example uses claude-opus-5-5. Neither page gives a price or a rough cost per run, and neither mentions that a cheaper model could run the same examples. I had to ask how much my test script cost. Switching all six requests to claude-haiku-5-5 worked without other changes (apart from issue 5). Its listed price is about 40 times lower: $0.10 / $0.50 per million input / output tokens, compared with $4 / $20 for Opus 5.5.

Expected: A one-line note about cost when I make my first call.

Suggestion: In Get started, add something like: "This call costs a fraction of a cent. To keep experimenting cheaply, use claude-haiku-5-5." Link to pricing. The "Models overview" card under Next steps helps, but it appears only after the first call.

docs.title: 5. Prefill example uses a deprecated model (Medium)
docs.text:
Page: Using the Messages API, "Prefilling Claude's response"

What happened: The runnable example uses claude-opus-4-5-20251101 with max_tokens=1. The page explains that Opus 4.5 is deprecated and that current models return a 400 error for prefill. It then lists four steps to adapt the example, but gives no code for them. When I moved my scripts to Haiku 5.5, I had to rewrite this example myself: I added a system prompt asking for only the letter, removed the assistant message and raised max_tokens to 1024 so there was room for thinking. That version worked and returned C.

Suggestion: Show the current-model version as code next to (or instead of) the Opus 4.5 example. Then the first code a reader copies from this section runs on a model that isn't deprecated.

docs.title: 6. Snippets leave out import anthropic (Low)
docs.text:
Page: Using the Messages API (basic request, multi-turn, prefill and vision examples)

What happened: The Python snippets start with message = anthropic.Anthropic()... and have no import. On its own, each snippet fails with NameError. It worked for me only because I pasted it into my Get started file, which already had the import. The vision snippet includes import base64 and import httpx2 but still not import anthropic.

Suggestion: Make each snippet runnable when copied on its own, or say once at the top of the page that the examples assume import anthropic.

docs.title: 7. Python output differs from the page's JSON (Low)
docs.text:
Page: Using the Messages API (basic request and others)

What happened: The page shows JSON under "Output". In Python, print(message) prints a Python object instead, such as Message(id='msg_...', content=[TextBlock(...)], ...). It's the same data in a different format, which was briefly confusing.

Suggestion: In the Python tab, print message.model_dump_json(indent=2) to match the JSON, or add a note that Python prints the object form.

docs.title: 8. Vision: no way to see the image (Low)
docs.text:
Page: Using the Messages API, Vision section

What happened: The example downloads an image and Claude describes it, but I never saw the image, so I couldn't judge the description. I added code to save the image and open it in Preview.

Suggestion: Show the example image on the page next to the code, or link to it.

docs.title: 9. Outdated sample output (Low)
docs.text:
Page: Get started, sample output

What happened: The sample response suggests searching for "Renewable energy news 2025", which looks out of date in late 2026.

Suggestion: Regenerate the sample output, or use a prompt whose answer doesn't depend on the date.

docs.title: What worked well
docs.text:
• The first API call worked on the first try after setup.
  • The multi-turn and URL-image examples worked unchanged.
  • The prefill section clearly says which models accept prefill and lists the alternatives.
  • ant auth status clearly showed which credential was active and why. I just didn't know to run it.

docs.title: Friction log: Gemini API
docs.text:
Notes from building Kairos; to be expanded.

Things that slowed me down while getting started with the Gemini API and building the first version of Kairos on it. SDK: google-genai 2.14.0 (Python), Interactions API, model gemini-3.6-flash.

Format per entry: what I tried / what happened / what I expected / suggested fix. Entry numbers match my original log, so references elsewhere (for example in gemini_agent.py) stay valid. For how the API compares with Claude's, see PORTING.md.

docs.title: 16. Sending a function result back returns a 400 with no field-level detail
docs.text:
• Tried: After Gemini called create_calendar_event, sending the result on a follow-up create() call with input=[{"type": "function_result", "call_id": ..., "result": json.dumps(result)}].
  • Happened: Error code: 400 - {'error': {'message': 'Invalid input received.', 'code': 'invalid_request'}}, with no hint of which field was wrong. There was no worked example of the function-calling round trip to check against: only the managed-agent and plain-text paths had samples.
  • Expected: Either an error naming the bad field, or a documented example of a complete function-call round trip.
  • What fixed it: Sending result as the raw dict instead of a json.dumps() string, and adding the optional name field with the function's name. The type stub accepts a str, but it's listed last in the union, and it isn't what the backend wants. Both changes were made together, so which one mattered (or both) isn't confirmed.
  • Suggested fix: A function-calling round-trip sample in the Interactions docs, and field-level detail in invalid_request errors.

docs.title: 8. Different parameter names in the Models API and the Interactions API
docs.text:
• Tried: Moving code between generate_content() and interactions.create().
  • Happened: One takes contents=, the other takes input=. Nothing flags the difference, so it's an easy copy-paste mistake.
  • Expected: Consistent naming, or a migration note.
  • Suggested fix: A short "coming from generate_content" table on the Interactions page.

docs.title: 9. The response JSON in the docs doesn't connect to the sample code
docs.text:
• Tried: Matching the documented response to what the code prints.
  • Happened: The docs show the full interaction object (id, status, usage, steps, ...), but the sample prints interaction.output_text, a derived field. When the wording of a reply changed, it looked like a bug rather than normal model variation read through a convenience property.
  • Expected: The sample to say where output_text comes from.
  • Suggested fix: One sentence linking output_text to the steps it summarizes.

docs.title: 5. Reasoning models return parts the sample code doesn't expect
docs.text:
• Tried: The quickstart sample with gemini-3.6-flash.
  • Happened: The model returns a thought_signature part alongside the text, and the SDK warns when .text drops it. The sample predates this and doesn't explain it.
  • Expected: Samples that match current models' output.
  • Suggested fix: Update the sample, or explain the warning next to it.

docs.title: 15. A 429 can mean two different things
docs.text:
• Tried: Following the quickstart's "watch for a 429" guidance, which describes it as the free-tier rate limit.
  • Happened: A run returned 429 with "Your prepayment credits are depleted": a billing problem that waiting won't fix. Same status code, different cause and fix. The runtime error message was more helpful than the docs: it named the cause and linked to where to fix it.
  • Expected: The docs to cover both meanings.
  • Suggested fix: List both 429 causes and how to tell them apart from the message.

docs.title: 1. The API key export silently disappears
docs.text:
• Tried: export GEMINI_API_KEY=... as the docs say.
  • Happened: It only lasts for the current terminal. A new window has no key, with no warning. (This came up again while building Kairos: an editor opened before the export can't see the key either.)
  • Expected: The docs to say how long the export lasts, and how to make it stick.
  • Suggested fix: One line on adding it to the shell profile (~/.zshrc).

docs.title: 2. No "did it work?" check for the key
docs.text:
• Tried: Confirming the key was set.
  • Happened: Nothing suggests a check. Typing echo GEMINI_API_KEY without the $ prints the variable's name, which looks exactly like "it's not set": a false negative for anyone new to the shell.
  • Expected: A documented check.
  • Suggested fix: Suggest a check that doesn't print the key, such as [ -n "$GEMINI_API_KEY" ] && echo set.

docs.title: 3. No minimum Python version stated
docs.text:
• Tried: pip3 install -U google-genai on Python 3.9.
  • Happened: The install succeeded silently. The problem only appeared later as a runtime FutureWarning that Python 3.9 is past end of life.
  • Expected: The minimum version stated before install.
  • Suggested fix: Put the supported Python versions at the top of the quickstart.

docs.title: 7. Version checks can mislead from an old environment
docs.text:
• Tried: pip index versions google-genai to find the latest release.
  • Happened: It reported 1.47.0 as latest: true only for the Python 3.9 environment it ran in, because pip hides versions that need a newer Python. That caused an extended false alarm that the Interactions API didn't exist.
  • Expected: A way to see the true latest version, or a note about this.
  • Suggested fix: A troubleshooting entry: "Can't find the Interactions API? Check your Python version first."

docs.title: 4. Unexplained NotOpenSSLWarning on macOS
docs.text:
• Tried: Running the quickstart with the Python that ships with macOS.
  • Happened: macOS's Python uses LibreSSL instead of OpenSSL, and urllib3 v2 warns about it.
  • Expected: The quickstart to anticipate the most common Mac setup.
  • Suggested fix: A note recommending a python.org or Homebrew Python on macOS.

docs.title: 6. Model names and APIs move faster than the docs
docs.text:
• Tried: Following a single snapshot of the docs.
  • Happened: During this work, the quickstart model changed from gemini-2.5-flash to gemini-3.6-flash, and a new API (Interactions) appeared. Any doc snapshot, even one fetched live, needed checking against the installed package.
  • Expected: Docs and the installed SDK to agree.
  • Suggested fix: Show the SDK version each page was written for.

docs.title: Beyond Kairos: managed agents
docs.text:
These came from the managed-agents quickstart, which Kairos doesn't use.

  • 10. No latency warning for remote sandboxes. environment="remote" starts a fresh sandbox VM per call, which is much slower than a text completion. The docs don't say this call behaves differently in kind.
  • 11. File retrieval is easy to miss. The "Download files from the environment" section exists, further down the page ("no SDK method yet"), but working top to bottom you hit a dead end after creating a file. A forward reference where files are first created would save the detour.
  • 12. "Download the file" downloads the whole sandbox. The endpoint returns a tar archive of the entire environment, not one file.
  • 13. The download endpoint isn't in the SDK. You build the URL, the x-goog-api-key header, and the alt=media parameter by hand with requests. A real SDK coverage gap, not only a docs gap.
  • 14. The docs' download sample fails on Python 3.12+. Unfiltered tarfile.extractall() tries to recreate device nodes and fails with PermissionError on macOS. The obvious fix, filter="data", is too strict for this archive (SpecialFileError on overlay artifacts). filter="tar" works. It took three tries, with no guidance in the docs.

docs.title: Friction log: MCP Python SDK
docs.text:
Notes from building Kairos; to be expanded.

Things that slowed me down while building Kairos's MCP server (mcp_server.py, Path 2). SDK: mcp 2.3.0 (Python).

Format per entry: what I tried / what happened / what I expected / suggested fix.

docs.title: 1. Most examples online use an API that no longer exists
docs.text:
• Tried: from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP, as most tutorials show.
  • Happened: ModuleNotFoundError. In 2.x, FastMCP was renamed to MCPServer (from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer). To its credit, the error message names the new import and links to the migration guide.
  • Expected: The tutorials I found to match the current major version.
  • Suggested fix: Keep the error message as it is (it's a model of how to break an API kindly), and put the version prominently at the top of examples.

docs.title: 2. Returning a dict doesn't give structured output
docs.text:
• Tried: A tool annotated -> dict, then reading result.structured_content in a client.
  • Happened: structured_content was None. The dict arrived as JSON text in result.content[0].text. Structured output needs a more specific return type.
  • Expected: A plain dict return to count as structured, or a warning that it doesn't.
  • Suggested fix: Say in the @tool() docs which return types produce structured output, with a dict example.

docs.title: 3. An uncaught exception reaches the model as a generic message
docs.text:
• Tried: Letting preview_event raise ValueError on a bad time string.
  • Happened: The client got is_error: true with only "Error executing tool preview_event", so the model had nothing to correct.
  • Expected: The exception message passed through, or guidance on how to return one.
  • Suggested fix: Document the pattern for model-readable tool errors. Kairos now catches the error and returns a message saying what's wrong and the expected format.

docs.title: 4. An MCP server can't ask the user "y/n"
docs.text:
• Tried: Reusing Path 1's input() confirmation step in the server.
  • Happened: Not possible: stdin and stdout carry the protocol. Any print() to stdout (including the mock calendar's) corrupts it.
  • Expected: This to be called out early for people coming from command-line agents.
  • Suggested fix: A "human approval in MCP servers" pattern in the docs. Kairos uses a preview tool plus a one-time confirmation id, and prints only to stderr.

docs.title: Porting a tool-calling agent from Gemini to Claude
docs.text:
Kairos was first built on Gemini's Interactions API and then ported to Claude's Messages API. This page compares the two, step by step, using the real code in gemini_agent.py and claude_agent.py. Everything the agents share (the tool schema, the system prompt, date handling, and the confirmation step) lives in calendar_tools.py and didn't need porting.

Versions: google-genai 2.14.0 and anthropic 2.13.0 (Python).

This page is about Path 1, where you write the agent loop yourself. Path 2 needs no porting at all: the MCP server works with any MCP client.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Step Gemini (Interactions API) Claude (Messages API) Client genai.Client() reads GEMINI_API_KEY anthropic.Anthropic() reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Call client.interactions.create(...) client.messages.create(...) User input input= messages=[{"role": "user", ...}] System prompt system_instruction= system= Tool schema key parameters input_schema "The model wants a tool" A step with type == "function_call" in interaction.steps stop_reason == "tool_use" and a tool_use block in content Tool arguments function_call.arguments tool_use.input Sending the result function_result with call_id, name, result tool_result with tool_use_id, content Result format The raw dict A string (Kairos sends JSON) or content blocks Conversation state Kept by the server: pass previous_interaction_id Kept by you: resend the whole conversation Required output limit Not required max_tokens

docs.title: 1. Defining the tool
docs.text:
Both APIs describe tool arguments with JSON Schema, so Kairos defines the schema once (TOOL_PARAMETERS) and wraps it for each API:

GEMINI_TOOL = {
    "type": "function",
    "name": TOOL_NAME,
    "description": TOOL_DESCRIPTION,
    "parameters": TOOL_PARAMETERS,
}

CLAUDE_TOOL = {
    "name": TOOL_NAME,
    "description": TOOL_DESCRIPTION,
    "input_schema": {**TOOL_PARAMETERS, "additionalProperties": False},
    "strict": True,
}

Differences:

  • Key name: parameters vs. input_schema.
  • Type field: Gemini's tool needs "type": "function". Claude's custom tools don't need a type.
  • Strict mode: strict: True makes Claude's arguments always match the schema. It requires additionalProperties: false, which is why the Claude wrapper adds it.

docs.title: 2. The system prompt
docs.text:
Both agents send the same prompt from build_system_prompt(): today's date, your timezone, and the source boundary. Only the parameter name changes:

# Gemini
client.interactions.create(model=..., system_instruction=system, tools=[GEMINI_TOOL], input=user_input)

# Claude
client.messages.create(model=..., max_tokens=16000, system=system, tools=[CLAUDE_TOOL],
                       messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_input}])

Claude requires max_tokens, a ceiling on the reply's length.

docs.title: 3. Detecting a tool call
docs.text:
Gemini returns a list of steps. A tool call is one of them:

function_call = next(
    (step for step in interaction.steps if step.type == "function_call"), None
)

Claude says why it stopped in stop_reason, and the tool call is a block in content:

if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    tool_use = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")

On current Claude models, content can also include thinking blocks before the tool_use block, so always select blocks by type, never by position.

docs.title: 4. Sending the result back
docs.text:
This is where the two APIs differ most.

Gemini keeps the conversation on its servers. You send only the new message and point at the earlier interaction:

client.interactions.create(
    model=GEMINI_MODEL,
    previous_interaction_id=interaction.id,
    input=[{
        "type": "function_result",
        "call_id": function_call.id,
        "name": function_call.name,
        "result": result,              # the raw dict
    }],
)

Claude's Messages API is stateless. You resend the whole conversation: the user's request, Claude's full reply (thinking blocks included), and your result:

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": user_input},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": response.content},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{
        "type": "tool_result",
        "tool_use_id": tool_use.id,
        "content": json.dumps(result),  # a string
    }]},
]
client.messages.create(model=model, max_tokens=16000, system=system,
                       tools=[CLAUDE_TOOL], messages=messages)

Watch the result format. Gemini wanted the raw dict: a JSON string caused a 400 (Gemini friction log #16). Claude's tool_result.content takes a string or content blocks, so the dict is JSON-encoded. Code copied across from one agent to the other breaks in both directions.

docs.title: 5. When the model doesn't call the tool
docs.text:
If a required detail is missing, both models reply with text instead.

Gemini Claude How you know No function_call step stop_reason == "end_turn" Reading the text interaction.output_text Join the text blocks in content Safety refusal (not handled in Kairos) stop_reason == "refusal"

docs.title: 6. Error handling
docs.text: Gemini agent Claude agent What Kairos does Checks for the key up front, then prints any API error's message instead of a traceback Checks for the key up front, then catches the SDK's typed exceptions and prints a readable message Exceptions used AuthenticationError, NotFoundError (bad model id), BadRequestError, RateLimitError, APIStatusError, APIConnectionError Retries The SDK retries rate limits and server errors automatically (2 retries by default) Observed gotchas A bad request shape returned Invalid input received. with no field named (#16). A 429 can mean a rate limit or depleted credits (#15).

docs.title: 7. Behavior differences seen in testing
docs.text:
These come from the same requests sent to both agents. They're observations from a small number of runs, not benchmarks.

  • Extraction quality was the same. On the 20-case eval, both scored 20/20 (recording).
  • Timezones: same moment, different form. For "3pm Eastern", Gemini returned 15:00-05:00, and Claude converted it to 12:00-08:00. Both are correct, which is why the eval compares moments, not strings.
  • Titles vary. For the same request, Gemini wrote "Q1 Roadmap Meeting" and Claude wrote "Q1 Roadmap Review". The eval doesn't score titles.
  • Reporting the result. On the mock calendar (which returns no event link), Claude said the event came from a test system and might not be on the calendar. Gemini said "I have scheduled the meeting." Both got the same result object.
  • Ambiguous dates. For "next Friday", both picked Dec 11 in the eval. In a separate live run, Claude asked which Friday was meant instead.

docs.title: Porting checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Rename system_instruction to system, and add max_tokens.
  • [ ] Wrap the schema in input_schema; add additionalProperties: false if using strict: true.
  • [ ] Replace "find the function_call step" with "check stop_reason, find the tool_use block".
  • [ ] Replace previous_interaction_id with a messages list you keep and resend.
  • [ ] Send the whole assistant content back, not just the text.
  • [ ] Change the result from a raw dict to a string (json.dumps).
  • [ ] Match tool_use_id, not call_id.
  • [ ] Read text by block type; don't assume content[0] is text.
  • [ ] Handle refusal as well as end_turn.
  • [ ] Re-run the eval on both and compare.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Plain-language definitions of the terms used in Kairos's code and docs. Stuck on an error instead? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Path 1 and Path 2. Kairos's two ways to use the same tool. In Path 1 you run an agent loop you wrote yourself (Quickstart). In Path 2 an MCP client like Claude Code runs the loop (Use Kairos over MCP). See Which path should I choose?

Agent. A program where a language model decides what to do next, such as calling a tool or asking a question, instead of following a fixed script.

Tool (or function). Something your code can do that the model can ask for. Kairos has one tool, create_calendar_event. The model never runs the tool itself. It asks, and your code decides whether to run it.

Messages API / Interactions API. The APIs Kairos calls: Claude's Messages API and Gemini's Interactions API. Both support tool calling; PORTING.md compares them.

Tool calling (function calling). The model replying with "call this tool with these arguments" instead of plain text. Claude calls this tool use; Gemini calls it function calling.

Tool schema. A description of a tool's arguments: their names, types, and which are required. It's written in JSON Schema, a standard format for describing JSON data. The model reads it to know what to fill in.

Arguments. The values the model fills in when it calls a tool, for example start_datetime and attendees.

System prompt. Instructions sent with every request that set the model's behavior, separate from what the user typed. Kairos's system prompt states today's date and your timezone.

stop_reason. A field in Claude's response saying why it stopped. tool_use means it wants to call a tool; end_turn means it replied with text, such as a question.

tool_result. The message your code sends back to Claude with the tool's output, so it can write its final reply.

Human approval gate (confirmation step). A point where the program stops and asks you before doing something with real effects. In Kairos it's Create this event? (y/n).

Mock backend. A stand-in for the real calendar that prints the event instead of creating it. It's the default, so you can experiment safely.

Source boundary. An instruction telling the model what it may treat as fact. Kairos tells it to use only details from your request and never invent an email, link, or agenda.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol). An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data. You write a tool once as an MCP server, and any app that speaks MCP can use it.

MCP server. A program that offers tools to AI apps. Kairos's is mcp_server.py; see Use Kairos over MCP.

MCP client. The AI app that connects to servers and uses their tools, such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop. In Path 2, the client runs the agent loop for you.

stdio transport. The client starts the server as a program and they exchange messages over its standard input and output. That's why an MCP server must never print to standard output.

Tool annotations. Hints a server gives about a tool, such as "read-only" or "reaches the outside world", so a client can decide how carefully to treat it.

Confirmation id. In Kairos's MCP server, a one-time code returned by preview_event. create_event only creates an event that was previewed with that code.

docs.title: Evals
docs.text:
Eval (evaluation). A repeatable test of how well a model does a task (run Kairos's). Unlike a normal test, a model can pass on one run and fail on the next.

Extractor. Anything that turns a request into event details. The eval scores three: the no-AI baseline, Claude, and Gemini.

Case. One test input with its expected result. Kairos's cases are in evals/cases.jsonl, one per line (add your own).

Golden set. A fixed collection of cases with known-correct answers. Kept fixed so results can be compared over time.

Check. One thing scored for a case, such as "are the attendees right?" A case passes only if all its checks pass.

Pass rate. The share of cases (or case runs) that passed.

Baseline. A simple, non-AI way of doing the same task, scored the same way. If the model can't beat it on a field, the model isn't needed for that field. Kairos's is evals/baseline_extractor.py.

Made-up-field rate. The share of tool calls containing a detail the request didn't support, like an email address that wasn't in it. Lower is better. It's this project's measure of hallucination: a model stating something with no basis in its input.

Ablation. Running the eval with one thing removed (here, the source boundary) to measure how much that thing helps.

Held-out set. Cases you don't look at while improving your prompt, used only to check. It shows whether an improvement is real or just tuned to the cases you watched (how to keep one).

Flaky case. A case that passes on some runs and fails on others. Find them with --repeat.

Saturated eval. One where everything scores (nearly) 100%. It can no longer tell models or prompts apart, so it needs harder cases.

Replay. Scoring saved model responses again, without calling the model. Free and instant, so you can change scoring rules or cases and see the effect.

LLM-as-judge. Using a model to grade answers that can't be checked by exact matching, such as "was that clarifying question helpful?" It's only trustworthy once you've measured how often it agrees with people.

docs.title: Dates and setup
docs.text:
RFC3339. The standard date-time format the tool uses, for example 2026-12-02T14:00:00-08:00. The ending -08:00 is the UTC offset: how many hours the local time is behind (or ahead of) UTC.

IANA timezone. A timezone name like America/Los_Angeles. Unlike abbreviations such as PST, it knows when daylight saving starts and ends. See Change your timezone.

Environment variable. A named setting, like CLAUDE_MODEL (choose a model), that a program reads when it starts. Used for API keys so they're never written into the code.

Virtual environment (venv). A private folder of Python packages for one project, so projects don't interfere with each other.

OAuth. The "sign in with Google and allow access" flow. Kairos uses it only for the real Google Calendar backend (set it up).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Kairos is a learning project for people who want to build their first AI agent and learn to evaluate it, but haven't known where to start.

If agents and evals feel like something only AI specialists build, this project is meant to change that. The whole agent is a few hundred lines of plain Python. The eval is one script you can run for free. Every piece is small enough to read in one sitting and change yourself.

Kairos is built mainly on Claude. The same agent is also built on Gemini, to show that once you understand the pattern, moving it to another LLM API is a small job, not a rewrite.

docs.title: Why a calendar?
docs.text:
The example agent turns a plain-English request ("45 minutes with alice@example.com tomorrow at 2pm") into a calendar event. That's the example, not the point. Scheduling was chosen because it's a good teacher:

  • Everyone understands the task, so you can focus on how the agent works rather than on the domain.
  • The output is checkable. A date is right or wrong, which makes it ideal for learning evals.
  • It has real stakes. An event sends invites to real people, so you learn why an agent should ask before it acts.
  • It has a classic weak spot. Models are confidently wrong about dates and timezones, which shows what code should own instead.

Swap the calendar for a support ticket, a database query, or an email draft, and every idea below still applies.

docs.text:
Skill What it means Where to see it in Kairos Build a tool-calling agent Describe a tool to the model, let it fill in the arguments, run the tool in your code, send the result back claude_agent.py Add a human approval gate Stop and ask the user before the agent does anything with real effects run_tool_call() in calendar_tools.py Let code own what code does best The model reads language; code does date math and timezones normalize_datetime() in calendar_tools.py Write your first eval A fixed set of test requests, each with the answer you expect, scored automatically evals/ Check whether you need an LLM at all Score a simple non-AI baseline the same way, and see where the model actually earns its cost evals/baseline_extractor.py Measure made-up answers Count how often the model fills in a detail the request never gave The made-up-field rate in evals/run_evals.py Read results, not just scores See pass rates, failures, token usage, and trends on a dashboard evals/dashboard.py and the eval dashboard Run the same agent on another LLM API Keep the shared logic, change only the API calls gemini_agent.py and Claude and Gemini side by side Expose a tool over MCP Turn the same tool into a server that any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop) can use mcp_server.py and Use Kairos over MCP Package it for others (advanced) Bundle the MCP server, a slash command, and a skill as a Claude Code plugin Bundle Kairos as a Claude Code plugin

As you go, Kairos tracks what you've done and awards five badges, from First Agent to Kairos Complete. Run python progress.py any time to see where you are.

docs.title: How an agent works, in six steps
docs.text:
Every tool-using agent follows the same loop. Here it is with Kairos as the example.

  1. The user asks for something. "45 minutes with alice@example.com tomorrow at 2pm to discuss Q3 planning."
  2. Your code sends the request to the model, along with a description of a tool: its name, what it does, and the arguments it takes. Kairos has one tool, create_calendar_event.
  3. The model decides. If it has what it needs, it replies by asking to call the tool, with the arguments filled in. If something required is missing (here, usually an email address), it asks the user instead.
  4. Your code checks and confirms. The model never runs anything itself. Your code checks the arguments (Kairos fixes timezones, and rejects a missing field or an end time before the start), shows them to the user, and waits for y.
  5. Your code runs the tool. Kairos creates the event, on a mock calendar by default.
  6. Your code sends the result back to the model, which tells the user what happened in plain language.

That's it. Kairos asks the model for one tool call at a time, which keeps the loop easy to follow. Bigger agents add more tools and repeat steps 3 to 6 in a loop, but the pattern doesn't change.

docs.title: Two paths: with and without MCP
docs.text:
Kairos lets you use the same tool in two ways. The difference is who runs the loop above.

Path 1: Build the agent yourself Path 2: Use the tool over MCP You run python claude_agent.py Claude Code or Claude Desktop, with mcp_server.py Who runs the loop Your code, step by step The MCP client Approval gate Create this event? (y/n) in your terminal preview_event, then create_event with a one-time id (only the newest preview counts) Today's date and timezone In the system prompt From a current_time tool What you learn How an agent works under the hood How to make a tool reusable by any AI app 
                     calendar_tools.py
        (field descriptions · dates · summary · calendars)
                 /                           \

   your loop, Claude Messages API       Claude Code / Desktop runs the loop

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data. Write a tool once as an MCP server, and any MCP client can use it, without the client's developers writing code for your tool.

docs.title: Which path should I choose?
docs.text:
Ask yourself one question: am I building my own app, or adding a capability to an AI app I already use?

Choose Path 1 (build the agent yourself) if:

  • You're new to agents and want to see what happens at every step
  • You're building your own program: a script, a backend service, a bot
  • You want full control of the prompt, the approval step, logging, and errors
  • You want to measure the agent with the eval (it tests Path 1 directly)
  • You have an Anthropic API key, and don't use Claude Code or Claude Desktop

Choose Path 2 (MCP) if:

  • You already use Claude Code or Claude Desktop and want it to schedule meetings
  • You want one tool that several AI apps can use
  • You'd rather not write or maintain an agent loop
  • You don't have an Anthropic API key: the server makes no model calls itself, so your existing Claude Code or Claude Desktop sign-in is enough
Path 1: build the agent Path 2: MCP You write The loop and the tool Only the tool You need An Anthropic API key Claude Code or Claude Desktop Who controls the prompt You (build_system_prompt()) The client, plus the server's instructions How you approve Type y in the terminal Approve the tool call in the client's chat Measured by the eval Yes, directly Partly: same field descriptions, but the client adds its own prompt Best for Learning how agents work; building your own app Extending an AI app you already use

Not sure? Do Path 1 first, then Path 2. Writing the loop yourself once makes it clear what an MCP client does for you. After that, Path 2 is mostly setup: your tool code stays the same.

docs.title: How an eval works
docs.text:
An eval answers one question: how often does the agent get it right?

  1. Write down test requests and the answers you expect. Kairos has 20, in evals/cases.jsonl. Three are deliberately incomplete; the right answer for those is a question, not a tool call.
  2. Run each request through the model, but stop before anything happens. The eval captures the tool arguments from step 3 above and never touches a calendar.
  3. Compare what the model returned with what you expected, field by field: attendees, start, end, Zoom link, agenda.
  4. Run a simple baseline the same way. If plain pattern matching scores as well on a field, the model isn't needed for it.
  5. Read the failures. The point of an eval isn't the score. It's learning why each case failed.
  6. Run it again, and watch the trend. Models aren't fully predictable, so --repeat 3 shows which cases are flaky. The eval dashboard charts every run, including the tokens each one used, so you can see whether a change helped and what it cost.

You can run the baseline and replay a saved Claude run without an API key, so you can explore all of this for free before spending anything. Today's results, and what they show, are in Run the eval.

docs.title: Why a confirmation step
docs.text:
The model writes to your calendar and emails invites to real people, so a wrong guess has a cost. Every event is shown in plain language, with times converted to your own timezone, before anything is created. Only an explicit y proceeds. Anything else cancels, and the model is told you declined, so it doesn't claim the event exists. Converting times for display matters too: if the model picks the wrong offset, you see a wrong-looking local time before saying yes, not after the invite goes out. Details that can't be right, such as a missing field or an end before the start, are caught before you're asked at all.

Over MCP there's no terminal to type y into, so the same gate is two tools: a preview that creates nothing, then a create step that accepts only the newest preview, once. Why the gate is two tools.

docs.title: Why code handles the dates
docs.text:
Models are good at reading "next Monday after lunch" and less reliable at date arithmetic and UTC offsets. So the work is split:

  • The prompt states today's date, your timezone, and its current UTC offset. The model has no other way to know what "tomorrow" means. (Over MCP, the current_time tool provides the same facts.)
  • The code normalizes every time the model returns. A time without an offset is given your timezone instead of silently becoming UTC. Daylight saving is resolved by Python's zoneinfo: March 15, 2027 correctly becomes -07:00 while December stays -08:00. The eval checks both.

docs.text:

Most of the code isn't tied to any provider. The two agent files are the only parts that change between Claude and Gemini, and they're about 120 to 150 lines each, including comments. Read them side by side to see how little changes. The README lists every file in the repo.

docs.title: Key ideas
docs.text:
The model never runs your tool. It only asks. Your code decides whether to run it, which is what makes an approval gate possible.

One tool schema, two wrappers. The tool's arguments are described once, in JSON Schema (TOOL_PARAMETERS). Each provider wants it wrapped slightly differently, so CLAUDE_TOOL and GEMINI_TOOL each add their own few lines.

The system prompt gives the model facts it can't know. The model has no idea what today's date is or which timezone you're in, so Kairos tells it. The prompt also sets a source boundary: use only what's in the request, and never invent an email or link.

Safe by default. The mock calendar is the default, so nothing you try sends a real invite. Switch to Google Calendar only when you're ready.

Evals compare meaning, not text. 3pm Eastern and 12pm Pacific are the same meeting, so the eval compares moments in time, not strings.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Clone Kairos, try it without an API key, then schedule your first meeting with Claude. Everything here uses the mock calendar: nothing is sent to a real calendar, and no invites go out.

New to some of the terms? See the Glossary.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • Python 3.11 or later. Check with:
python3 --version

If it says 3.10 or lower, or "command not found", install a current Python from python.org/downloads.

On a Mac, check this even if Python is installed. macOS includes an older Python (3.9), and python3 may point to it. After installing a newer one, run its versioned command instead, for example python3.12 --version, and use python3.12 in place of python3 in step 1. - git, to download the code. Check with git --version. - An Anthropic API key, for step 4 only. Steps 1 to 3 work without one. Get a key at console.anthropic.com under API Keys. Model calls cost money; this whole quickstart costs a few cents.

On Windows, use PowerShell, and type python wherever this page says python3.

docs.title: 1. Download and install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/archjayas/kairos.git
cd kairos
python3 -m venv .venv

The last line creates a virtual environment: a private folder (.venv) for this project's packages, so they don't mix with anything else on your computer. Turn it on:

source .venv/bin/activate          # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1         # Windows PowerShell (if it says scripts are disabled,
                                   # run: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned)

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). Run the activate command again whenever you open a new terminal for this project. Then install the packages:

pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 2. Try the eval, free (no API key)
docs.text:
The eval checks how well something turns a request into event details. The baseline is plain pattern matching, with no AI, so it runs instantly and for free:

python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline

You'll see a table of 20 test requests, each marked PASS or FAIL, then a summary and an explanation of every failure. The baseline gets 17 of 20. The three it misses are the ones that need a model: a time in another timezone, and agendas the baseline's simple patterns can't spot.

docs.title: 3. See how Claude did, free (no API key)
docs.text:
The repo includes a saved run of Claude and Gemini on the same 20 requests. Replay scores it again without calling any model:

python evals/run_evals.py --replay evals/recordings/sample_run.json

Both models pass all 20. Compare their column with the baseline's to see where the model earns its cost. Run the eval explains every column.

To see the same results as charts, open them in the dashboard:

python evals/dashboard.py --results evals/recordings/sample_run.json

docs.title: 4. Schedule a meeting with Claude
docs.text:
Now you need your API key. Set it, plus the model to use, in your terminal:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="paste-your-key-here"     # macOS / Linux
export CLAUDE_MODEL="claude-opus-5-5"

$env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "paste-your-key-here"     # Windows PowerShell
$env:CLAUDE_MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

These are environment variables: settings the program reads when it starts. Keeping the key there means it's never written into the code. They last until you close the terminal. To keep them, see Troubleshooting. To use a different Claude model, see Switch models.

Run the agent:

python claude_agent.py

At Your request:, paste this and press Enter:

Schedule a meeting with alice@example.com and bob@example.com tomorrow at 2pm for 45 minutes to discuss Q3 planning. Zoom link: https://zoom.us/j/123456789

Claude reads the request and fills in the event details. Before anything is created, you'll see a summary like this, with tomorrow's date:

About to create this event:
  Title:     Q3 Planning Discussion
  Start:     Tue Dec 1, 2026 2:00 PM PST      (your date will be tomorrow's)
  End:       Tue Dec 1, 2026 2:45 PM PST
  Attendees: alice@example.com, bob@example.com
  Agenda:    Discuss Q3 planning.
  Zoom link: https://zoom.us/j/123456789
Create this event? (y/n)

Check the date and time, then type y. The mock calendar prints the event it would have created, and Claude confirms in plain language.

docs.title: 5. Say no, and leave something out
docs.text:
• Say no. Run it again and type n. Nothing is created, and Claude offers to change something.
  • Leave something out. Try "Set up a 30 minute sync with Alice tomorrow at 3pm." There's no email address, so Claude asks for one instead of guessing.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
1. Your request went to Claude, together with a description of a tool called create_calendar_event.
  2. Claude replied by asking to call that tool, with the details it found: title, times, attendees, agenda, Zoom link.
  3. Kairos's code checked the times, showed you the summary, and waited for your y.
  4. The result went back to Claude, which wrote the confirmation you read.

That loop is the core of every tool-using agent. The Overview explains it step by step, and claude_agent.py is the code: about 150 lines with comments, worth reading top to bottom.

You just used Path 1: an agent loop you run yourself. Kairos has a second path.

docs.title: 6. Optional: the same tool in Claude Code (Path 2)
docs.text:
In Path 2 you don't run an agent script. Claude Code runs the loop, and Kairos's tools reach it through an MCP server (mcp_server.py). If you have Claude Code installed, from the kairos folder run:

claude

Approve the kairos MCP server when asked, type /mcp to check it's connected, then ask Claude Code to schedule the same meeting. It shows you a preview first and creates nothing until you approve. See Use Kairos over MCP for details, Claude Desktop, and debugging.

On Windows, first change command in .mcp.json to .venv\\Scripts\\python.exe (JSON needs each backslash written twice).

docs.title: See your progress
docs.text:
Kairos notices what you've done. After steps 2 and 4 you've earned your first badge, First Agent: you'll see a message when it happens. To see all your badges and what's next:

python progress.py

See Progress and badges for the full list, and See your progress for every way to check.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text: Kairos follows semantic versioning: the first number changes for breaking changes, the second for new features, the third for fixes.

docs.title: 0.1.0 (Nov 23, 2026)
docs.text: The first public version.

docs.title: Path 1: build the agent yourself
docs.text:
• A Claude agent (claude_agent.py) on the Messages API with tool use. Try it in the Quickstart.
  • The same agent on Gemini (gemini_agent.py), to show how an agent moves between LLM APIs (compare them).
  • A human approval step: nothing is created until you type y.
  • Dates and timezones handled in code, including daylight saving.
  • A mock calendar by default; Google Calendar when you opt in.

docs.title: Path 2: use the tool over MCP
docs.text:
• An MCP server (mcp_server.py) with current_time, preview_event, and create_event, usable from Claude Code or Claude Desktop (how).
  • A two-step approval gate: an event can only be created after it's been previewed, unchanged, with a one-time confirmation id.

docs.title: Evals
docs.text:
• 20 test cases, scored field by field (run the eval), with a made-up-field rate.
  • A no-AI baseline scored the same way, to show where the LLM earns its cost.
  • --repeat to find flaky cases, --no-boundary to measure the source-boundary instruction, and --replay to score a saved run with no API key.

docs.title: Dashboard and progress
docs.text:
• An eval dashboard (evals/dashboard.py): pass rate, accuracy per check, made-up fields, token usage, every case, and pass rate over time.
  • Token usage recorded for every live eval run.
  • Progress and badges: Kairos records your milestones locally and awards five badges (python progress.py).

docs.title: Docs
docs.text: • This website, an overview, a quickstart, ten how-to guides, a glossary, troubleshooting, a Claude/Gemini comparison, and friction logs for three APIs.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The 20 cases are cleanly written, and both models currently score 100%, so the eval can no longer tell them apart. Harder cases are next.
  • The agents handle one tool call per reply, so a request for two meetings books only one. Ask for the second separately.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
docs.text: Each answer quotes the exact message you'll see. New to a term? See the Glossary.

docs.title: No matching distribution found for anthropic==... during pip install
docs.text:
Cause: your virtual environment was made with a Python that's too old. Kairos needs Python 3.11 or later. On macOS, python3 often points to the built-in Python 3.9.

Fix: delete the old environment and make a new one with a newer Python:

deactivate                      # if the environment is active
rm -rf .venv
python3.12 -m venv .venv        # or whichever 3.11+ version you installed
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version                # should say 3.11 or later
pip install -r requirements.txt

Don't have 3.11 or later? Install it from python.org/downloads.

docs.title: My API key is set, but the agent says it isn't
docs.text:
Symptom: export worked in one terminal, but the agent (or your editor) can't see the key. For Gemini you'll see:

ValueError: No API key was provided. Please pass a valid API key.

Cause: export only applies to the terminal you ran it in. Other terminals, and apps like VS Code that were already open, don't see it.

Fix: add the key to your shell profile, then open a new terminal:

echo 'export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"' >> ~/.zshrc      # bash: ~/.bashrc

Check that it saved without printing the key: grep -c GEMINI_API_KEY ~/.zshrc should print 1. If you work in VS Code, quit it fully (Cmd+Q on macOS) and reopen it so it reads the profile again.

docs.title: Set CLAUDE_MODEL to a Claude model id
docs.text:
The Claude agent doesn't hard-code a model. Set one:

export CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5

See Switch models.

docs.title: Model '...' not found: check CLAUDE_MODEL
docs.text:
The id is misspelled, retired, or not available to your key. List the ones you can use:

python -c "import anthropic; [print(m.id) for m in anthropic.Anthropic().models.list()]"

docs.title: Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to your key from console.anthropic.com.
docs.text: The Claude agent checks for your key before asking for a request. Set it (see My API key is set, but the agent says it isn't if you already did). The Gemini agent shows the same kind of message for GEMINI_API_KEY.

docs.title: Authentication failed: check ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
docs.text: The key is set, but it's mistyped or revoked. Create a new one at console.anthropic.com and set it again.

docs.title: I ran out of usage credits
docs.text:
Model calls are paid from your API account, so an empty balance stops them. What you'll see:

  • Claude agent: Bad request: ... with a message saying your credit balance is too low.
  • Gemini agent: Gemini API error: ... with a 429 saying your prepayment credits are depleted. A 429 can also mean a rate limit, which clears if you wait; a credits 429 doesn't.
  • The eval: every call to that model fails, followed by Warning: every claude call failed. The run isn't saved, so your last good results are kept.

Add credits in console.anthropic.com (Plans & Billing) or, for Gemini, in aistudio.google.com, then run the step again. To avoid surprises, set a monthly spend limit in the same place.

While you top up, the free steps still work: --models baseline and --replay make no model calls, and Path 2 uses your Claude Code or Claude Desktop plan, not API credits.

docs.title: zsh: command not found: code
docs.text: That's the VS Code shell command, which isn't installed by default on macOS. In VS Code, open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) and run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH. You don't need it for this project.

docs.title: The time is off by a few hours
docs.text:
TIMEZONE probably doesn't match where you are. It defaults to America/Los_Angeles:

export TIMEZONE=America/New_York

See Change your timezone.

docs.title: TIMEZONE='...' isn't a timezone Kairos recognizes
docs.text: TIMEZONE must be a Region/City name like America/Chicago, not a word like Pacific. Avoid abbreviations too: some, like EST, are accepted but ignore daylight saving. See Change your timezone.

docs.title: "Next Friday" picked a different Friday than I meant
docs.text: It's ambiguous: on a Tuesday, "next Friday" can mean this week's or next week's. Models sometimes ask and sometimes pick one. Check the date in the confirmation summary before typing y, or say the date: "Friday, December 11."

docs.title: The model asked a question instead of creating the event
docs.text: That's intended when a required detail is missing, usually an attendee email. The model is told never to invent emails. Run it again with the details it asked for.

docs.title: The model says the event was created, but it's not on my calendar
docs.text: You're on the mock backend, the default. It prints the event instead of sending it. Set CALENDAR_BACKEND=google to write to your real calendar; see Use your real Google Calendar.

docs.title: I typed yes and it cancelled
docs.text: Only y creates the event, in either case and ignoring spaces. Anything else, including yes, cancels. That's deliberate: a confirmation step that guesses what you meant isn't a confirmation step.

docs.title: /mcp doesn't list kairos, or says it failed to start
docs.text:
• Start Claude Code in the kairos folder. It reads .mcp.json from the folder it starts in.
  • Create the virtual environment first. .mcp.json runs .venv/bin/python, so .venv must exist with the packages installed (see the Quickstart).
  • On Windows, change command in .mcp.json to .venv\\Scripts\\python.exe (JSON needs each backslash written twice).
  • Still failing? Use the absolute path to the Python inside .venv. See Use Kairos over MCP.

docs.title: Unknown, already-used, or replaced confirmation_id
docs.text: Only the newest preview can be created, and each one only once. If you asked for a change, Claude previews again, and the earlier preview is cancelled. Ask Claude to preview the event again, then approve it.

docs.title: Claude created the event without asking me
docs.text: You've probably allowed create_event to run without approval. Remove that permission in Claude Code so it asks every time; the server's two-step gate relies on it. See why the gate is two tools.

docs.title: FileNotFoundError: ... credentials.json
docs.text: With CALENDAR_BACKEND=google, the app needs an OAuth client file. Either save it as credentials.json in the directory you run from, or point to it with GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_FILE. See Use your real Google Calendar.

docs.title: It worked before, but now authorization fails
docs.text: The saved token in token.json expired or was revoked. Delete it and run again; a browser window asks you to approve access once more.

docs.title: Error 403: access_denied in the browser
docs.text: Your OAuth consent screen is in testing mode and your account isn't listed as a test user. Add it under OAuth consent screen → Test users in the Google Cloud console.

docs.title: ValueError: Unknown CALENDAR_BACKEND '...'
docs.text: Only mock and google are supported.

docs.title: Skipping gemini: set GEMINI_API_KEY to run it.
docs.text: The eval skips any model it can't call: claude needs CLAUDE_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and gemini needs GEMINI_API_KEY. baseline always runs. If nothing is left to run, the eval says so and suggests --models baseline.

docs.title: Unknown --models ...
docs.text: Model names are baseline, claude, and gemini, separated by commas, for example --models baseline,claude.

docs.title: Warning: every claude call failed
docs.text: Every call to that model returned an error, usually a wrong API key or model id. Check the error messages above the warning. The run isn't saved, so your last good results and your trend chart aren't affected, and it doesn't count toward the Evaluator badge.

docs.title: A case passed last time and failed this time
docs.text: Models aren't fully deterministic, and by default each case runs once. Look at the "Why each failure failed" section and evals/results/latest.json to see what the model returned. Run with --repeat 3 to see how often each case passes. If a case keeps changing, it's telling you the request is ambiguous.

docs.title: Does the eval create calendar events?
docs.text: No. It stops after the model's first turn and never calls the confirmation step or any calendar backend, mock or real.

docs.title: Progress and badges
docs.text: For every way to check your progress, see See your progress.

docs.title: Do I need to rebuild the site to see a new badge?
docs.text:
No. Preview the site with mkdocs serve and leave it running: when you earn a badge, the page reloads by itself within a second or two. If it doesn't, stop mkdocs serve (Ctrl+C) and start it again.

A published site (mkdocs build or mkdocs gh-deploy) never shows your personal badges, so rebuilding or republishing won't change it. That's deliberate: your progress stays on your computer.

docs.title: The home page shows all five badges in color, but I haven't earned them
docs.text: You're looking at a published or built copy of the site, which shows the badges as a preview of what you can earn. To see your own, run mkdocs serve and open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Opening files from the site/ folder directly shows the preview too.

docs.title: I did the step, but the badge didn't unlock
docs.text:
Check what Kairos recorded:

python progress.py --no-open

Then compare with what counts for each milestone:

  • Free eval: run_evals.py with --models baseline or --replay.
  • Claude agent: claude_agent.py has to reach Claude's final reply after the confirmation step. If you stopped it early (Ctrl+C), or Claude asked a question instead of calling the tool, it doesn't count. Run it again with a complete request.
  • Live eval: run_evals.py has to call Claude or Gemini. Replay doesn't count here, because it makes no model calls.
  • MCP: an event has to be created through the MCP server. Previewing isn't enough; approve the create_event call.
  • Gemini: gemini_agent.py has to reach Gemini's final reply, or the eval has to run --models gemini.

The First Agent badge needs two milestones: the free eval and the Claude agent.

docs.title: My badges disappeared
docs.text: Progress is saved in .kairos/progress.json inside the project folder. A new clone, a deleted .kairos folder, or python progress.py --reset starts you over. If you set KAIROS_PROGRESS_FILE, Kairos reads and writes that file instead, so check it's set the same way each time.

docs.title: Is my progress sent anywhere?
docs.text: No. It's a small file on your computer, it's git-ignored so it isn't committed, and nothing in Kairos uploads it.

docs.title: How do I start over?
docs.text: python progress.py --reset

docs.title: Add a field to the tool
docs.text: This guide adds an optional room field (a meeting room name) as an example. The same steps work for any field. Because both agents share one schema, you change calendar_tools.py and both agents pick it up.

docs.title: 1. Add it to the schema
docs.text:
In calendar_tools.py, add a property to TOOL_PARAMETERS["properties"]:

"room": {
    "type": "string",
    "description": "Meeting room name, only if the request names one.",
},

Leave it out of required. If you make a field required, the model has to supply it, so it either asks every time or invents a value.

Write the description for the model, not for people. It's the only guidance the model gets about when to fill the field. "Only if the request names one" discourages made-up values.

docs.title: 2. Put it on the event
docs.text:
In build_event_body(), add a room=None parameter and decide where it goes. Google Calendar has no room field for personal calendars, so add it to the description:

if room:
    description_parts.append(f"Room: {room}")

Note that location already holds the Zoom link when there is one.

docs.title: 3. Pass it through
docs.text:
• Add room=None to create_calendar_event() and pass it to build_event_body().
  • In run_tool_call(), pass room=args.get("room").
  • For Path 2, add a room parameter to preview_event() in mcp_server.py, annotated with Field(description=FIELD["room"]), and include it in args. The description comes from the schema you edited in step 1, so you don't write it twice.

docs.title: 4. Show it at confirmation
docs.text:
In format_event_summary(), add a line so you can check the value before saying y:

f"  Room:      {args.get('room') or '(none)'}",

docs.title: 5. Test it
docs.text:
• By hand: run either agent with "... in the Redwood room", and once without a room, to check the model leaves it out.
  • In the eval: add "room" to the expected fields of a few cases and a check in score() in evals/run_evals.py. To count invented rooms in the made-up-field rate, extend made_up_fields() as well.

Claude's tool uses strict: true, which requires additionalProperties: false. CLAUDE_TOOL adds that for you, so you don't need to change it.

docs.title: Add eval cases
docs.text: Each line of evals/cases.jsonl is one test case in JSON. Add a line, run the eval, and the new case is scored like the others.

docs.title: Case format
docs.text:
A request the model should act on:

{"id": "c21", "category": "relative_date", "request": "Same day next week at 9am with dana@example.com for 30 min to review the budget.", "expect_call": true, "expected": {"attendees": ["dana@example.com"], "times": [["2026-12-08T09:00:00-08:00", "2026-12-08T09:30:00-08:00"]], "zoom_link": null, "agenda": true}}

A request the model should not act on, because something required is missing:

{"id": "c22", "category": "incomplete", "request": "Book the usual sync with the design team.", "expect_call": false}
Field Meaning id Unique id, shown in the results table category Free-text label for grouping (relative_date, zoom, incomplete, ...) request Exactly what a user would type expect_call true if the model should call the tool, false if it should ask instead clarify_ok Optional. true if asking a question also counts as a pass expected.attendees Every email that should be invited, lowercase expected.times A list of acceptable [start, end] pairs, in RFC3339 with offsets expected.zoom_link The exact link, or null if the request has none expected.agenda true (must be present), false (must be absent), or null (not scored)

Remember that "today" is Tuesday, 2026-12-01, in America/Los_Angeles. The model is told the date but not the time of day, so avoid requests like "in two hours" that depend on the current time. Work out expected dates from that, and check the UTC offset for the event's date, not today's.

docs.title: Write cases that teach you something
docs.text:
A case that every extractor already passes doesn't add much. Good new cases are ones you're not sure about:

  • Messy phrasing: typos, "EOD Thursday", "after lunch tomorrow" (decide what you'd accept, or set "clarify_ok": true if asking is the right answer)
  • Relative dates that need care: "same day next week at 3pm", "the 1st"
  • Links without a label: a Zoom URL pasted at the end with no "Zoom:" in front
  • Two people named but only one email given
  • Requests where the right answer is a question, not a guess

docs.title: Keep a held-out set
docs.text:
If you tune the prompt while watching the same cases, you'll overfit to them. Keep a second file that you don't look at while making changes, and run it only to check:

python evals/run_evals.py --cases evals/heldout.jsonl --out evals/results/heldout.json

docs.title: Check your case before running the models
docs.text:
Run the free baseline first. It catches typos in the JSON and in expected times without spending any API calls:

python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline

docs.title: Change your timezone
docs.text: Relative times like "tomorrow at 3pm" are resolved in the timezone set by TIMEZONE. The default is America/Los_Angeles.

docs.title: Set it
docs.text:
Use an IANA timezone name: Region/City, not an abbreviation.

export TIMEZONE=Europe/London
python claude_agent.py
Use Not America/New_York EST, Eastern Europe/Berlin CET Asia/Kolkata IST UTC GMT+0

Abbreviations are a trap: some, like PST, are rejected, but others, like EST, load and then ignore daylight saving, so your times are an hour off for half the year. Always use Region/City. To find yours, run python -c "import zoneinfo; print(sorted(zoneinfo.available_timezones()))".

docs.title: What the setting changes
docs.text:
• The system prompt tells the model today's date in that timezone and its current UTC offset.
  • Times without an offset that the model returns are interpreted in that timezone.
  • The confirmation summary shows times converted to that timezone, so you can check them before saying y.
  • Google Calendar events are created with that timeZone.

docs.title: Meetings in another timezone
docs.text: You don't need to change TIMEZONE for a one-off. Say it in the request: "3pm Eastern with sam@example.com." The model returns a time with the Eastern offset, and the summary shows it in your own timezone (12:00 PM if you're on Pacific time).

docs.title: Daylight saving
docs.text: Offsets are calculated for the event's date, not today's. In America/Los_Angeles, a meeting on March 15, 2027 gets -07:00 even if you schedule it in December, when the offset is -08:00. The eval includes a case that checks this.
