docs.title: Bundle Kairos as a Claude Code plugin
docs.text:
A Claude Code plugin packages tools and instructions so anyone can install them with two commands. This guide bundles Kairos's MCP server (Path 2), a /schedule-meeting command, and a skill into one plugin, then shows how to use it in the terminal and in VS Code.

This is an advanced guide. Do Use Kairos over MCP first: a plugin is mostly that same MCP server, packaged.

docs.title: What's in a plugin
docs.text:
kairos/
  .claude-plugin/
    plugin.json            # name, version, description
    marketplace.json       # lets this folder be installed as a plugin source
  .mcp.json                # the MCP server the plugin starts (already in the repo)
  commands/
    schedule-meeting.md    # the /schedule-meeting slash command
  skills/
    kairos-scheduling/
      SKILL.md             # when and how Claude should use the Kairos tools
  mcp_server.py, calendar_tools.py, ...   # the code the server runs
Piece What it adds MCP server The tools: current_time, preview_event, create_event Command A slash command that runs a fixed prompt, like /schedule-meeting Skill Instructions Claude loads when a task matches, for example "always preview first"

docs.title: 1. Describe the plugin
docs.text:
Create .claude-plugin/plugin.json:

{
  "name": "kairos",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Schedule meetings from plain English, with a preview-then-confirm approval gate.",
  "author": { "name": "Your Name" },
  "keywords": ["calendar", "mcp", "agent", "learning"]
}

And .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, so the folder can be installed directly:

{
  "name": "kairos-marketplace",
  "owner": { "name": "Your Name" },
  "plugins": [
    { "name": "kairos", "source": "./", "description": "Kairos calendar tools over MCP." }
  ]
}

docs.title: 2. Point the MCP server at the plugin's folder
docs.text:
When a plugin is installed, Claude Code copies it to its own plugin folder. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is that folder's path, so use it instead of relative paths.

The server also needs Python with the mcp package. The simplest way to give an installed plugin its own packages is uv, which installs them on the fly. Replace .mcp.json with:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kairos": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "--with", "mcp==2.3.0", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/mcp_server.py"],
      "env": { "CALENDAR_BACKEND": "mock" }
    }
  }
}

If you'd rather not use uv, point command at a Python that already has the packages, using an absolute path such as /Users/you/kairos/.venv/bin/python. That only works on your own computer.

This changes Path 2's setup

The repo's current .mcp.json uses .venv/bin/python, which works when you open the project folder in Claude Code. The plugin version above works from anywhere, but needs uv. Pick one, and update Use Kairos over MCP to match.

docs.title: 3. Add a slash command
docs.text:
Create commands/schedule-meeting.md:

---
description: Schedule a meeting from a plain-English request, with a preview first
allowed-tools: mcp__plugin_kairos_kairos__current_time, mcp__plugin_kairos_kairos__preview_event
---

Schedule this meeting: $ARGUMENTS

1. Call `current_time` to get today's date and the user's timezone.
2. Call `preview_event` with the details from the request. Use only details the user
   gave; if an attendee email is missing, ask for it instead of guessing.
3. Show the user the summary from `preview_event`, word for word, and ask whether to
   create the event.
4. Only if they say yes, call `create_event` with the `confirmation_id`.

allowed-tools lets the command run the two read-only tools without asking. create_event is deliberately left out, so Claude Code still asks you before anything is created. That keeps the approval gate.

Tool names follow the pattern mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>; here both the plugin and the server are called kairos.

docs.title: 4. Add a skill
docs.text:
A skill is guidance Claude loads automatically when a task matches its description, so it applies even without the slash command. Create skills/kairos-scheduling/SKILL.md:

---
name: kairos-scheduling
description: Use when the user asks to schedule, book, or set up a meeting or calendar event.
---

When scheduling with the Kairos tools:

- Call `current_time` before turning "tomorrow" or "next Friday" into dates.
- If "next Friday" or a similar phrase could mean two dates, ask which one.
- Always call `preview_event` first and show its summary. Never call `create_event`
  until the user has seen the summary and said yes.
- Never invent attendee emails, links, or agendas.

docs.title: 5. Install it and try it
docs.text:
In Claude Code, from any folder:

/plugin marketplace add /absolute/path/to/kairos
/plugin install kairos@kairos-marketplace

The first command registers the folder as a plugin source; the second installs the plugin from it. Restart Claude Code, then:

  1. Type /mcp: kairos should be connected, with three tools.
  2. Try /schedule-meeting 30 minutes with alice@example.com tomorrow at 2pm about the launch.
  3. Approve create_event when asked.

An installed plugin runs from Claude Code's own copy, so its progress is saved there, not in your repo. To count it toward your Connector badge, add "KAIROS_PROGRESS_FILE": "/absolute/path/to/kairos/.kairos/progress.json" to the server's env in .mcp.json.

To share it, push the repo to GitHub. Others install it with /plugin marketplace add archjayas/kairos, then the same /plugin install line.

docs.title: Use it in VS Code
docs.text:
Claude Code's VS Code extension uses the same plugins. Once you've installed the plugin in Claude Code, open the Claude Code panel in VS Code and the kairos tools, /schedule-meeting, and the skill are available there too. You don't need a separate VS Code extension.

To use the server with VS Code's own AI features (for example, agent mode in Copilot Chat) instead of Claude Code, VS Code can start MCP servers listed in .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "kairos": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["${workspaceFolder}/mcp_server.py"],
      "env": { "CALENDAR_BACKEND": "mock" }
    }
  }
}

That gives VS Code the tools only. The slash command and skill are Claude Code features.

A real VS Code extension (a .vsix on the Visual Studio Marketplace) is a separate, larger project: an extension written in TypeScript that registers the MCP server with VS Code. Start from VS Code's documentation on MCP servers in extensions if you want to go that far. For Kairos, the plugin above covers both the terminal and VS Code.

docs.title: Check before you share
docs.text:
• [ ] create_event is not in any command's allowed-tools.
  • [ ] .mcp.json sets CALENDAR_BACKEND to mock, so new users can't send real invites by accident.
  • [ ] No credentials.json, token.json, or .env in the plugin folder.
  • [ ] /mcp shows three tools after a fresh install.

docs.title: Publish the site
docs.text: The Kairos website, with its home page of cards, search, and dark mode, is built from the Markdown files in docs/ with Material for MkDocs. The result is a folder of plain HTML that you can host anywhere.

docs.title: 1. Install the site tools
docs.text:
These are separate from the agent's packages. With your virtual environment active:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt

docs.title: 2. Set your repo URL
docs.text:
In mkdocs.yml, change repo_url to your repository:

repo_url: https://github.com/your-username/kairos

Every link to a code file on the site is built from this one line. (The docs link to code with relative paths like ../claude_agent.py, which work on GitHub. mkdocs_hooks.py turns them into GitHub links when the site is built.)

docs.title: 3. Preview it locally
docs.text:
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. The page reloads as you edit any file in docs/.

docs.title: GitHub Pages (one command)
docs.text:
mkdocs gh-deploy

This builds the site and pushes it to a gh-pages branch. In your repository on GitHub, go to Settings → Pages and set the source to the gh-pages branch. The site appears at https://your-username.github.io/kairos/.

docs.title: Any other host
docs.text:
mkdocs build --strict

This writes the whole site to a site/ folder. Upload that folder to any static host, such as Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, or a plain web server. On hosts that build for you, use:

Setting Value Build command pip install -r requirements-docs.txt && mkdocs build --strict Output folder site

--strict stops the build on any broken link or missing page, so a broken site never gets published. site/ is git-ignored; it's rebuilt every time.

docs.text:
1. Create the Markdown file in docs/ (or docs/how-to/).
  2. Add it under the right tab in nav: in mkdocs.yml, so it appears in the menu.
  3. To show it on the home page, add a link to the right card in docs/index.md. The cards are grouped by audience: Start here (beginner), Go further (advanced), and Help and updates. Keep each card to a handful of links; if one grows past five or six, it's probably two cards.

docs.title: Run the eval
docs.text: The eval measures how well each model extracts event details from a request. It sends 20 fixed requests to each extractor, captures the tool arguments from the first turn, and scores them. It never runs the confirmation step or touches any calendar.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
From the repo root:

python evals/run_evals.py                          # every extractor with credentials set
python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline        # free: no API keys, no network
python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline,claude

An extractor is anything that turns a request into event details: the no-AI baseline, Claude, or Gemini. The eval scores each one the same way.

Extractor Needs baseline Nothing. It's regex and the standard library. gemini GEMINI_API_KEY (and optionally GEMINI_MODEL) claude ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and CLAUDE_MODEL (choose one)

Claude is skipped if CLAUDE_MODEL isn't set, and Gemini if GEMINI_API_KEY isn't. A full run is about 40 model calls and costs well under a dollar.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option What it does --models baseline,claude,gemini Which extractors to run (default: all three) --replay FILE Score saved responses instead of calling models. Free; try evals/recordings/sample_run.json --repeat N Run each case N times, to find flaky cases that pass on some runs and fail on others --no-boundary Leave the "use only what's in the request" instruction out of the prompt, to measure what it's worth --cases FILE Use a different case file, such as a held-out set --out FILE Where to save results (default evals/results/latest.json)

docs.title: What gets scored
docs.text:
"Today" is pinned to Tuesday, 2026-12-01, in America/Los_Angeles (the model is told the date, not the time), so results don't change with the date you run them.

Check Passes when attendees The set of emails matches exactly (order and case ignored) start, end The times are the same moment as expected (15:00-05:00 equals 12:00-08:00) zoom_link It matches the link in the request, or is absent when there isn't one agenda It's present when the request gives a topic, absent when it doesn't, unscored when it's unclear no_call On an incomplete request, the model asked instead of calling the tool

A case passes only if all its checks pass. For the ambiguous case (c17, "next Friday"), either Friday is accepted, and so is asking which one was meant.

The made-up-field rate is the share of tool calls that include an email or Zoom link not in the request, or an agenda the request never gave. Lower is better.

docs.title: Read the output
docs.text:
The run prints three things:

  1. A table: one row per case, PASS or FAIL: <checks> per extractor.
  2. A summary: the pass rate and per-check accuracy for each extractor.
  3. "Why each failure failed": expected vs. actual for every failed check.

Full results, including every model's tool arguments and token usage, are written to evals/results/latest.json. Use --out to write elsewhere.

To see the results as charts, with token usage and pass rate over time, run python evals/dashboard.py. See Eval dashboard.

docs.title: Latest results
docs.text:
From the saved run (Claude claude-opus-5-5, Gemini gemini-3.6-flash). See them as charts on the eval dashboard.

Metric Baseline (no AI) Claude Gemini Cases passed 17/20 20/20 20/20 Start / end time 16/17 17/17 17/17 Agenda 7/9 9/9 9/9 Attendees, Zoom link 100% 100% 100% Asks when info is missing 3/3 3/3 3/3 Made-up-field rate 0% 0% 0%

What this shows. The baseline matches both models on emails, Zoom links, durations, and simple dates. The models earn their cost on two things: times in another timezone ("3pm Eastern") and agendas the baseline's patterns can't spot ("We'll walk through the Q4 incident report..."). It also shows the limits of the set: both models score 100%, so these cases can no longer tell them apart. The next step is harder cases.

docs.title: What the eval doesn't measure
docs.text:
• The reply text. Only the tool arguments are scored, not how well the model words its question or confirmation.
  • The event title. Titles vary legitimately ("Q3 Planning" vs. "Q3 Planning Discussion"), so they're not compared.
  • Consistency, unless you ask. By default each case runs once, and a case that passes on one run can fail on the next. Use --repeat 3 to find those flaky cases.
  • Hard inputs. The 20 cases are cleanly written. Both models currently score 100%, which means the set can no longer tell them apart. Add harder cases.

docs.title: See your progress
docs.text:
Kairos keeps track of what you've done as you learn, and awards five badges along the way. You don't have to log anything: the scripts notice when you reach a milestone and save it on your computer.

There are three ways to see where you are. All of them read the same progress file.

Way Command Best for In the terminal python progress.py --no-open A quick check Your progress page python progress.py Seeing your journey and badges at a glance On the Kairos site mkdocs serve Your badges on the site's home page, updating live

Run every command from the kairos folder, with your virtual environment active (see the Quickstart).

docs.title: When you earn a badge
docs.text:
You don't need to check: the moment a step unlocks a badge, the script you ran says so.

🏅 Badge earned: First Agent! See your progress: python progress.py

docs.title: 1. In the terminal
docs.text:
python progress.py --no-open

You'll see a progress bar, each milestone with the date you reached it, each badge, and what to do next:

Kairos progress  [####................]  1 of 5 badges

  [x] Ran the eval for free (baseline or replay)  (2026-11-23)
  [x] Completed a full tool call with the Claude agent  (2026-11-23)
  [ ] Ran the eval on a live model
  [ ] Scheduled a meeting through the MCP server
  [ ] Ran Kairos on another LLM (Gemini)

  🚀  First Agent: earned
  🔒  Evaluator: Run the eval on a live model.  ->  python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline,claude
  ...

Next up: Evaluator. Run the eval on a live model. Try: python evals/run_evals.py --models baseline,claude

docs.title: 2. Your progress page
docs.text:
python progress.py

This prints the same summary, then opens a page in your browser with:

  • A progress bar: how many of the five badges you have.
  • Your journey: one stop per milestone, filled in with the date you reached it.
  • What's next: the next badge, and the command to try.
  • Your badges: earned ones in color; locked ones in red, with how to earn them.

The page is saved as .kairos/progress.html. Run python progress.py again to refresh it after you earn something.

docs.title: 3. On the Kairos site
docs.text:
Preview the site on your computer, and your badges appear on the home page (under Your badges) and on the My progress tab:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt     # first time only
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Hover a badge to see what it's for, when you earned it, or how to earn it.

Leave mkdocs serve running. When you earn a badge, the page reloads by itself within a second or two. You don't need to rebuild anything.

docs.title: Why a published site shows a preview
docs.text: A published copy of the site (on GitHub Pages, for example) shows all five badges in color, marked as a preview. That's because your progress is saved on your computer, and a website on the internet can't read it. This is deliberate: your progress is never uploaded, and if you publish the site yourself, your personal badges aren't included.

docs.title: What gets recorded
docs.text:
Milestone Recorded when Ran the eval for free run_evals.py runs with --models baseline or --replay Completed a full tool call with Claude claude_agent.py reaches Claude's final reply after the confirmation step (typing y or n both count) Ran the eval on a live model run_evals.py calls Claude or Gemini Scheduled a meeting through MCP The MCP server's create_event creates an event Ran Kairos on another LLM gemini_agent.py reaches Gemini's final reply, or the eval runs Gemini

Progress is saved in .kairos/progress.json in the project folder. It's git-ignored, so it's never committed, and nothing in Kairos sends it anywhere.

docs.title: Start over, or keep progress somewhere else
docs.text:
python progress.py --reset                          # forget all progress
export KAIROS_PROGRESS_FILE=~/kairos-progress.json   # save progress to another file

If you set KAIROS_PROGRESS_FILE, set it the same way every time, or Kairos reads a different file and your badges seem to disappear.

docs.title: Switch models
docs.text: Neither agent hard-codes a Claude model, and the Gemini model can be overridden.

docs.title: Claude
docs.text:
CLAUDE_MODEL is required. Set it to any current Claude model id:

export CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5      # most capable Opus
export CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5    # faster, lower cost
export CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5     # fastest, lowest cost

To see the ids your key can use:

python -c "import anthropic; [print(m.id) for m in anthropic.Anthropic().models.list()]"

An unknown id gives Model '...' not found: check CLAUDE_MODEL.

docs.title: Gemini
docs.text:
GEMINI_MODEL is optional and defaults to gemini-3.6-flash. Set it to any Gemini model id that supports function calling:

export GEMINI_MODEL=your-gemini-model-id

To see the ids your key can use:

python -c "from google import genai; [print(m.name) for m in genai.Client().models.list()]"

docs.title: Compare models on the same requests
docs.text:
Running the agent by hand shows one request at a time. To compare models properly, run the eval once per model and compare the summaries:

CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5   python evals/run_evals.py --models claude --out evals/results/opus.json
CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5  python evals/run_evals.py --models claude --out evals/results/haiku.json

See Run the eval for how to read the results.

docs.title: Use your real Google Calendar
docs.text:
By default, events go to a mock calendar that only prints them. This guide connects the agents to your primary Google Calendar.

Events created this way are real and send invites to the attendees. The confirmation step still applies: nothing is created without y.

docs.title: 1. Install the Google client libraries
docs.text:
These are already in requirements.txt. If you installed manually, run:

pip install google-api-python-client google-auth-oauthlib

docs.title: 2. Create an OAuth client
docs.text:
1. In the Google Cloud console, create or pick a project.
  2. Enable the Google Calendar API for that project.
  3. Configure the OAuth consent screen. For personal use, choose External and add your own Google account as a test user.
  4. Under Credentials, create an OAuth client ID of type Desktop app.
  5. Download the JSON file and save it as credentials.json in the folder you run Kairos from (the repo root, in these docs).

credentials.json is git-ignored. Never commit it or paste its contents anywhere.

docs.title: 3. Switch the backend
docs.text:
export CALENDAR_BACKEND=google
python claude_agent.py

The first time, a browser window asks you to grant access to your calendar. After you approve, a token.json is saved in the folder you run from, so you won't be asked again until the token expires or is revoked. token.json is also git-ignored.

The app asks only for the calendar.events scope: it can create and edit events, not change your calendar settings.

docs.title: Keep the files somewhere else
docs.text:
To keep credentials outside the repo, point to them with environment variables:

export GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_FILE="$HOME/.config/kairos/credentials.json"
export GOOGLE_TOKEN_FILE="$HOME/.config/kairos/token.json"

docs.title: Go back to the mock
docs.text: export CALENDAR_BACKEND=mock     # or: unset CALENDAR_BACKEND

docs.title: Revoke access
docs.text: Remove the app at myaccount.google.com/permissions and delete token.json.

docs.title: Use Kairos over MCP (Path 2)
docs.text:
In Path 1 you run claude_agent.py, an agent loop you wrote yourself. In Path 2 you don't write a loop at all. mcp_server.py offers Kairos's calendar tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and an MCP client, such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop, runs the agent for you.

Both paths share calendar_tools.py: the same field descriptions, date handling, summary, and mock calendar.

Not sure which path is for you? See Which path should I choose?

docs.title: What the server offers
docs.text: Tool What it does Changes anything? current_time Returns today's date, your timezone, and its UTC offset No preview_event Checks the event details, returns a plain summary and a one-time confirmation_id No create_event Creates a previewed event, given its confirmation_id Yes (mock calendar by default)

docs.title: Why the approval gate is two tools
docs.text:
Path 1 asks Create this event? (y/n) in the terminal. An MCP server can't do that: its standard input and output carry the protocol messages, so there's no terminal to type into. So the gate is split:

  1. preview_event returns exactly what would be created, and creates nothing.
  2. create_event only creates an event that was previewed, unchanged. Each confirmation_id works once, and only the newest preview can be created: if you ask for a change, the earlier preview is cancelled.

The model can't create anything you weren't shown. Whether you're asked in between is up to the client: Claude Code asks permission before running a tool unless you've allowed it. Don't auto-allow create_event, or the gate is gone.

docs.title: Why there's a current_time tool
docs.text: In Path 1, today's date and your timezone go in the system prompt. An MCP server doesn't control the client's prompt, so it offers the same facts as a tool, and its instructions tell the client to call it before working out "tomorrow at 3pm". Set your timezone with TIMEZONE in the server's env (see below, and Change your timezone).

docs.title: Use it from Claude Code
docs.text:
The repo includes a .mcp.json file, so Claude Code finds the server when you open the project:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kairos": {
      "command": ".venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["mcp_server.py"],
      "env": { "CALENDAR_BACKEND": "mock" }
    }
  }
}
  1. Finish the Quickstart setup, so .venv exists with the packages installed.
  2. Start Claude Code in the repo folder (claude). The first time, it asks whether to trust the project's MCP server. Approve it.
  3. Type /mcp to check that kairos is connected and shows three tools.
  4. Ask: "Schedule 45 minutes with alice@example.com tomorrow at 2pm to discuss Q3 planning."
  5. Claude calls current_time and preview_event, then shows you the summary. Say yes, and approve the create_event call when asked.

On Windows, change command in .mcp.json to .venv\\Scripts\\python.exe (JSON needs each backslash written twice). If Claude Code can't start the server, use the absolute path to the Python inside .venv instead.

To use your own timezone, add it to env, for example "TIMEZONE": "Europe/London".

docs.title: Use it from Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Claude Desktop starts servers listed in its config file. Open it from Settings → Developer → Edit Config, and add Kairos with absolute paths (Desktop doesn't start in your project folder):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kairos": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/kairos/.venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/kairos/mcp_server.py"],
      "env": { "CALENDAR_BACKEND": "mock", "TIMEZONE": "America/Los_Angeles" }
    }
  }
}

Restart Claude Desktop, then ask it to schedule a meeting.

docs.title: Debug it with the MCP Inspector
docs.text:
The MCP Inspector is a browser UI for calling a server's tools by hand, with no model involved. It needs Node.js:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector .venv/bin/python mcp_server.py

Try create_event with a made-up id (it's refused), then preview_event, then create_event with the id it returned (it works once).

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Never print() to standard output in an MCP server. Standard output carries the protocol, so a stray print corrupts it. Kairos's mock calendar prints to standard error for this reason.
  • Previews are kept in memory. If the server restarts, old confirmation_ids stop working. Preview again.
  • The real calendar works here too, after one setup step. Sign in to Google once outside MCP, by running CALENDAR_BACKEND=google python claude_agent.py from the repo folder (see Use your real Google Calendar). The sign-in can't happen inside the MCP server, because it needs your terminal and browser. Then set "CALENDAR_BACKEND": "google" in env, plus GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_FILE and GOOGLE_TOKEN_FILE as absolute paths (Claude Desktop doesn't start in your project folder). create_event then sends real invites, so keep approving it by hand.
